summary: Kole Jain breaks a UX case study into eight steps: define the problem with a short solution snapshot, make the case study look good, build data-backed user personas, map user flows, show lo-fi wireframes, present the final design with the reasoning beside it, reflect honestly, and add style through story, brevity and chapter-like titles. He walks through Emily Shen's portfolio case study as the running example. He says a case study has two goals: to show what problems you found and how you solved them, and to show what someone gets if they hire you. It matters to someone building a design system mainly as guidance on documenting and presenting design decisions and their reasons, not on choosing token values [inferred].
key_ideas: A case study should show the problem you found and how you solved it, and quietly show what a client or employer gets by hiring you.
Get the problem statement right first: if the problem is wrong or does not exist, the solution does not matter.
Put a brief summary of the solution at the top, so readers see problem and solution without scrolling to the bottom.
Research does not need to be hard: a Google Form sent to friends and family works, and an affinity map turns the data into common findings.
How the case study looks matters as much as what it says; concise text with lots of images and GIFs keeps people reading.
Charts need clear titles, axis titles and a legend, and circling and annotations help understanding.
A user persona exists to consolidate data and inform decisions, so focus on goals, frustrations, behaviour and pain points, not the photo or name.
Keep projects and user flows small; a smaller project lets you put more quality into it.
Lo-fi wireframes let you ideate rapidly and test assumptions with a couple of people before building a full prototype.
Show final designs large, with text beside each one explaining why you made those choices.
A reflection section that admits flaws, lessons and features left out makes the case study more genuine and you a more credible designer.
Tell the process as a story, keep it readable in one sitting, and use chapter-style titles so it can be skimmed.

topics.name: Portfolio and case studies
topics.summary: Gives an eight-step structure for a UX case study: problem and solution snapshot, strong presentation, data-backed personas, small user flows, lo-fi wireframes, final design with reasoning, reflection, and style (story, brevity, chapter-like titles).

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Describes the process a case study should reveal: collect data (even a Google Form), synthesise it in an affinity map into a problem statement, build a persona, map the user flow, sketch lo-fi wireframes, test them with a couple of people, tweak and retest, then design and reflect.

topics.name: Presenting designs
topics.summary: Presentation is as important as content: concise text, many images and GIFs, final designs shown large with explanatory text beside them, and clickable tabs as one way to organise screens.

topics.name: Dashboards and data display

rules.rule: Nail down a strong problem statement before anything else and open the case study with it; keep it clear and concise and back it with your research, as in the Emily Shen example.
rules.why: If you identify the wrong problem or a non-existent one, your solution won't matter at all.
rules.evidence: step number one is going to be to have a strong definition of the problem

rules.rule: Place a brief summary of the solution at the top, right after the problem, and expand on the process further down.
rules.why: Clients and employers don't want to scroll all the way to the bottom to find the solution.
rules.evidence: having a summary of your solution is a fantastic thing to put up top

rules.rule: Collect data (a Google Form sent to friends and family is enough), group it in an affinity map into common findings that become the problem statement, and show those summarized findings.
rules.why: Summarized findings really help to solidify the definition of the problem, and collecting data doesn't need to be difficult.
rules.evidence: Emily's Affinity map where she took all of her data

rules.rule: Keep case study text concise and include many images and GIFs that help explain it.
rules.why: Presentation is just as important as content; if it doesn't look good people aren't going to read it.
rules.evidence: step number two is to make your case study look nice

rules.rule: Give every chart a title, titles on the axes and a legend.
rules.why: How you portray data is very important and impacts how much people understand from your case study.
rules.evidence: include titles for everything to have titles on the axes and to include a legend

rules.rule: Use very clear graphs, and circle and annotate the parts of the data that matter.
rules.why: Clear graphs, circling and annotations help understanding of the data.
rules.evidence: even circling and including annotations is fantastic

rules.rule: Build user personas from your data and centre them on the user's goals and frustrations as they relate to your problem and solution.
rules.why: A persona exists to consolidate data and inform design decisions; otherwise it has no bearing on the final design.
rules.evidence: the biggest points to hit on are the goals and frustrations

rules.rule: Don't spend time on persona details like finding a photo or picking a name, or on extraneous details unrelated to the problem.
rules.why: Extraneous details generally serve no value and just waste time; behaviour, interests and pain points are what shape the design.
rules.evidence: not to get caught up on small details like finding a photo or picking a name

rules.rule: In user flows, use different shapes and colors to tell step types apart, for example orange for a decision, blue for a process the user does, and green for an input or output.
rules.why: Shapes and colors can be a nice way to differentiate between different pages.
rules.evidence: orange is for a decision variable blue is a process

rules.rule: Keep the project and its user flow small rather than giant.
rules.why: The smaller it is, the more quality you can put into it.
rules.evidence: look at just how small this user flow is

rules.rule: Make low-fidelity wireframes (hand-drawn or in Figma) before high fidelity, and include preliminary or incomplete sketches in the case study.
rules.why: Lo-fi lets you ideate rapidly toward the best layout, and rough sketches show readers your process.
rules.evidence: low Fidelity wireframes are very important

rules.rule: Test lo-fi wireframes by having a couple of people go through them, observe whether things are intuitive, tweak, and test again before moving to the final design.
rules.why: It lets you test assumptions without committing to a fully fledged prototype.
rules.evidence: grab a couple of people and make them go through your wireframe

rules.rule: Present each final design with text next to it explaining the design choices and why it solves the problem.
rules.why: The explanation of why you made your choices is what people end up looking at most.
rules.evidence: have the design with the text next to it to explain your design choices

rules.rule: Display design images as large as reasonably possible; don't squish many screens down.
rules.why: Squished screens hide the detail, so readers can't understand your design decisions.
rules.evidence: make sure you display your images nice and large

rules.rule: End with a brief reflection covering what could be better, difficulties you hit, what you learned, and features or sections left out for time.
rules.why: It makes the case study more genuine and makes you seem like a better designer, even if it highlights flaws.

rules.rule: If your research used friends and family, note in the reflection that a more diverse, representative sample is an improvement for next time.
rules.why: Starting out, friends and family are not a very diverse and representative sample; that is fine but can be improved.
rules.evidence: generally a good thing to improve on is your research method

rules.rule: Write the case study as a story, letting real moments (getting stuck, a method you had to use, a breakthrough from a tester) guide it.
rules.why: People don't like to read, but they love a good story; it adds personality and interest.
rules.evidence: making your case study sound like a story

rules.rule: Keep the case study short enough to read in one sitting, favouring videos and images over text.
rules.why: People don't like to read; think of the case study like a web page, where you limit text in favour of videos, images or other media.
rules.evidence: it should be readable in one sitting let's say 10 to 15 minutes

rules.rule: Make the case study skimmable with section titles that, like book chapter titles, summarize the content and make readers want to read more; avoid boring titles.
rules.why: Titles let readers skim and intrigue them to read on.
rules.evidence: make your case study skimmable with titles

decisions.question: Where should the solution appear in a case study?

options.name: Brief solution summary at the top
options.effect: Readers see the problem and then instantly see the solution; the process follows below.
options.when: Always, for clients or employers who skim.

options.name: Solution revealed only at the end
options.effect: Readers have to scroll all the way to the bottom to learn the outcome.

decisions.recommendation: Put a brief solution summary up top, because clients and employers don't want to scroll to the bottom to find it.
decisions.evidence: having a summary of your solution is a fantastic thing to put up top

decisions.question: How big should the project and its user flow be?

options.name: Small project, small user flow
options.effect: Fewer screens, each with more care and quality.
options.when: Default; you don't need a big project for a good case study.

options.name: Large project, giant user flow
options.effect: Massive case studies with giant user flows, and less quality can go into each part.

decisions.recommendation: Keep it small; the smaller it is, the more quality you can put into it.
decisions.evidence: you don't need a big project to make a good case study

decisions.question: How should step types be told apart in a user flow diagram?

options.name: Color and shape coding
options.effect: Orange marks a decision, blue a process the user does, green an input or output, so the flow reads at a glance.
options.when: Kole's favoured approach, mocked up in FigJam.

options.name: Uniform shapes
options.effect: All steps look the same, so types must be read from labels [inferred].
options.when: Not discussed; the source only recommends differentiation.

decisions.recommendation: Use different shapes and colors to differentiate steps.
decisions.evidence: using different shapes and colors can also be a nice way to differentiate

decisions.question: How should low-fidelity wireframes be made and shown?

options.name: Hand-drawn sketches
options.effect: Rough drawings with arrows and shading; fast to ideate.
options.when: If you prefer to draw, as Kole does.

options.name: Lo-fi wireframes in Figma
options.when: If you prefer working in Figma.

decisions.recommendation: Either works; include preliminary or even incomplete sketches because they add value and show your process.
decisions.evidence: whether you prefer to draw like me or want to hop on figma

decisions.question: How should final design screens be presented?

options.name: Large screens with explanatory text beside each
options.effect: Detail stays visible and the reasoning sits right next to the design; clickable tabs can group screens.
options.when: Default for the final design section.

options.name: Many screens squished together
options.effect: Detail is lost, so readers can't understand the design decisions.

decisions.recommendation: Show designs as big as reasonably possible with text next to them explaining the choices.
decisions.evidence: choosing to make it as big as reasonably possible is generally a good idea

decisions.question: What kind of section titles should a case study use?

options.name: Chapter-style titles
options.effect: Titles summarize the section and make readers intrigued to read more.

options.name: Plain, boring titles
options.effect: Sections are labelled but don't pull the reader in.

decisions.recommendation: Take inspiration from book chapter titles.
decisions.evidence: take some inspiration from chapters of books

decisions.question: What should a user persona contain?

options.name: Data-backed, problem-specific persona
options.effect: Goals, frustrations, behaviour, interests and pain points tied to the problem and solution; it informs the design.

options.name: Detailed persona with photo, name and extraneous details
options.effect: Looks fantastic but ultimately has no bearing on the final design and wastes time.

decisions.recommendation: Build the persona from your data and focus on goals and frustrations as they relate to your problem and solution; don't get caught up on the photo or name.
decisions.evidence: the biggest points to hit on are the goals and frustrations

decisions.question: How long should a case study be?

options.name: Short, readable in one sitting
options.effect: About 10 to 15 minutes of reading, with text limited in favour of videos and images.

options.name: Long and text-heavy
options.effect: Every detail written out; people don't like to read, so fewer will get through it.

decisions.recommendation: Keep it short: concision is your friend, and it should be readable in one sitting, around 10 to 15 minutes.
decisions.evidence: it should be readable in one sitting let's say 10 to 15 minutes

process.detail: Aim to show the problems you identified and how you solved them, and to show what people get if they hire you; every later step serves these.

process.step: 1. Define the problem and snapshot the solution
process.detail: Write a clear, concise problem statement backed by research, with a brief solution summary up top. Collect data (a Google Form to friends and family is enough), group it in an affinity map, and show summarized findings.
Keep text concise and use many images and GIFs. Present data with clear graphs, circling and annotations, and give charts titles, axis titles and a legend.
Make the persona from your data, focused on goals, frustrations, behaviour, interests and pain points tied to the problem; skip time on photo, name and extraneous details.
Mock the flow up (Kole uses FigJam) with shapes and colors for decisions, processes and inputs or outputs, and keep it small.

process.step: 5. Sketch lo-fi wireframes and test them
process.detail: Draw or use Figma to ideate layouts quickly, include rough sketches in the case study, have a couple of people go through them, observe what is intuitive, tweak and test again.

process.step: 6. Show the final design and the problems it solves
process.detail: Show designs large with explanatory text beside them (clickable tabs are one layout) explaining why the design solves the problem best.
Briefly cover what could be better, difficulties, what you learned, research-method improvements, and features left out for time.
Tell it as a story, keep it short enough to read in 10 to 15 minutes, and make it skimmable with chapter-like titles.
